content: Cervical cerclage is a surgical procedure where a stitch is placed around the uterine cervix to prevent it from shortening or opening prematurely. This intervention is intended to reduce the risk of preterm birth. However, its effectiveness and safety in pregnancies involving multiple fetuses remain uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether cervical cerclage improves obstetrical and perinatal outcomes in multiple pregnancies. This included cases where cerclage was performed due to a history of pregnancy loss (history-indicated cerclage), findings of a short cervix on ultrasound (ultrasound-indicated cerclage), or physical changes in the cervix detected during an examination (physical exam-indicated cerclage). The primary outcomes assessed were perinatal deaths, serious neonatal complications, and a combination of these two outcomes. The review included five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving a total of 1577 women, though only 128 women with multiple pregnancies (122 with twins and six with triplets) were analyzed. Two trials focused on history-indicated cerclage (73 women), while three trials examined ultrasound-indicated cerclage (55 women). The quality of the trials ranged from average to above average, though some had unclear risks of selection and detection biases. When the outcomes of all types of cerclage were combined and compared to no cerclage, there were no statistically significant differences in the rates of perinatal deaths (19.2% with cerclage vs. 9.5% without cerclage), serious neonatal morbidity (15.8% with cerclage vs. 13.6% without cerclage), or the combined outcome of perinatal death and neonatal morbidity (40.4% with cerclage vs. 20.3% without cerclage). Secondary outcomes also showed no significant differences between the cerclage and no cerclage groups. These included rates of preterm birth before 34 weeks, preterm birth before 35 weeks, low birthweight (<2500 g), very low birthweight (<1500 g), respiratory distress syndrome, cesarean section (both elective and emergency), and maternal side effects. Subgroup analysis revealed that ultrasound-indicated cerclage was associated with an increased risk of low birthweight, very low birthweight, and respiratory distress syndrome. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the small number of trials, significant heterogeneity, and differences between subgroups. None of the included studies reported on long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes for the infants. Additionally, no trials involving physical exam-indicated cerclage were available for comparison. In conclusion, based on limited data from five small studies of average to above average quality, there is no evidence to support the use of cervical cerclage as an effective intervention for preventing preterm births or reducing perinatal deaths and neonatal morbidity in multiple pregnancies.
